analysis.one_liner: Removes all campaign contribution limits, lets corporations and unions give directly, and ends public presidential campaign financing while adding disclosure rules.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted no cosponsors, never received a committee vote or a House floor vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have scrapped nearly every limit on money in federal elections. It would end the caps on what any individual can give to a candidate, lift the ban on corporations and labor unions donating directly from their treasuries, and shut down the taxpayer checkoff that finances presidential campaigns. In exchange, it would require all campaign reports to be filed electronically and posted online, force campaigns to disclose every contribution they get in the final 90 days of a race within 24 hours, and make state and local party committees file their state-level spending reports with the FEC. It was introduced by one representative with no cosponsors and never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy individuals would gain the most: with all contribution limits terminated after 2007, a single donor could give unlimited sums directly to candidates and parties. Corporations and labor unions would gain a channel that has been closed for a century, since the ban on using treasury money for federal elections would be repealed. Political parties would gain as unlimited-money intermediaries, and campaigns would gain from lighter limits overall. Challengers and third-party candidates, per the bill's own findings, were the intended beneficiaries, on the theory that current caps force them to scrape together thousands of small donors while incumbents and self-funding millionaires start with built-in advantages. Voters would also get faster, fuller disclosure: every report online, and every contribution in a race's final 90 days reported within 24 hours.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy donors, corporations, unions, and parties

how_it_helps.text: It removes all caps on contributions to federal candidates and parties after 2007, so donors could give any amount directly to the candidate of their choice.
It repeals the ban on corporate and labor union contributions and expenditures for elections after December 2007, allowing businesses and unions to fund candidates directly from their treasuries.

It requires all campaign reports to be filed electronically and posted on the internet, requires 24-hour reporting of every contribution received in the 90 days before an election, and requires state and local party committees to file copies of their state-law spending reports with the FEC — giving voters faster, fuller information about who is funding campaigns.

The bill's stated purpose, in its findings, is to help challengers compete with incumbents and wealthy self-funding candidates by letting them raise larger amounts from fewer supporters, and to reduce the reporting burden that the findings say favors well-financed interest groups.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary voters' relative influence would shrink: in a system with no contribution limits, a candidate's time and attention flows toward whoever can write the largest checks, and the 2007-era caps of a few thousand dollars per person would no longer put small donors on anything like equal procedural footing. The taxpayer-financed presidential system would end, removing the option of candidates who answer to public funding rather than private fundraisers. Candidates who rely on many small donors would compete against rivals who can be funded in full by a handful of large givers, corporations, or unions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ordinary voters, small donors, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill would remove all limits on campaign contributions and lift the decades-old ban on corporate and labor union treasury money in federal elections, allowing the largest donors and organized interests to give without cap and making their financial weight count for far more than an ordinary voter's.
It would end taxpayer-financed presidential campaigns, eliminating the public checkoff option that lets presidential candidates run without relying on private money.

The new reporting rules would require every contribution of any size received in the final 90 days before an election to be reported within 24 hours, and would remove the 'best efforts' flexibility for identifying contributors who give over $200, adding compliance work for campaign treasurers and small committees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The disclosure side of the bill is genuinely good: every committee filing online, 24-hour reporting near elections, and state party spending funneled through federal disclosure would give voters real information. But those improvements are outweighed by the bill's core trade: unlimited contributions in exchange for disclosure. Disclosure tells you after the fact who gave; limits constrain how much any one interest can give in the first place. Removing the corporate and union ban would also allow union dues and corporate treasuries — money contributed by people who may disagree — to fund campaigns directly. A bill built around that trade, with zero cosponsors and no committee action, offered the transparency improvements without the limits that give them meaning.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, neither ever acted on it, no other member cosponsored it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: H.R. 484 was introduced by Rep. John Doolittle on January 16, 2007 and referred to the House Administration Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the same day.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over its entire two-year lifespan.
The action history shows no further activity after the referral: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action in either committee's jurisdiction.
The bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, without ever coming to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Existing limits on campaign contributions, the ban on corporate and union treasury money in elections, and taxpayer-financed presidential campaigns all remained in place. Campaign finance transparency advocates also gained nothing, since the bill's electronic filing and 24-hour reporting provisions died with it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Contribution limits and the corporate donation ban survived

for.name: Rep. John T. Doolittle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 16, 2007; it received no cosponsors and no committee action.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the January 2007 referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill's provisions ending the presidential public financing checkoff after the referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a solo effort: one Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, so no partisan lineup ever formed around it.

industries.note: The bill repeals the ban on corporate contributions and expenditures in federal elections, letting companies fund candidates directly from treasury money. That would give organized business interests a direct channel to officeholders that has been closed since the 1907 Tillman Act era rules embodied in FECA.

With all contribution limits terminated, the largest individual donors could give unlimited sums to candidates and parties. The bill's own findings argue this helps challengers, but the practical effect is to amplify the political voice of the very rich relative to ordinary voters.

The same repeal lifts the ban on union contributions and expenditures, letting unions fund federal candidates directly from dues-based treasuries. Unions gain a channel alongside, not against, the corporate interests they usually oppose at the ballot box.

industries.industry: Public campaign financing (Presidential Election Campaign Fund)
industries.note: The bill terminates the $3 tax checkoff, the Presidential Election Campaign Fund, and the primary matching payment account, sweeping leftover money into the general treasury. This removes the one system that lets presidential candidates run without private fundraising.

Parties could accept unlimited contributions, but they take on new duties: electronic filing of all reports, 24-hour reporting of contributions in the final 90 days of a campaign, and filing state-level party spending reports with the FEC. The money is uncapped; the paperwork is heavier.
